newsitem.title: GERMANY: Dollar surge turns up heat on G7 in Berlin.
newsitem.headline: Dollar surge turns up heat on G7 in Berlin.

text.p: Foreign exchange markets pitted their collective will against the world's financial leaders on Friday, pushing the dollar up by two pfennigs against the mark even as the officials headed to Berlin for a summit.

Currency issues had already looked set to dominate the meeting, with officials from the Group of Seven leading industrial nations disturbed by recent rapid dollar gains, but in a quandary over how to slow the rise without tipping the market into reverse.
But the fresh surge instilled new urgency into the meeting of finance ministers and central bank governors.
In Washington, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin responded to the sharp gains by signalling that the United States was willing to talk about the dollar's strength.

In a subtle departure from the U.S. position that a strong dollar was desirable, Rubin indicated it may be time for slight shift in stance. "A strong dollar is in the U.S. interest. We've had a strong dollar for some time," he said.
Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer declined comment on Friday's dollar rise as he arrived in Berlin and the Canadian delegation also refused to be drawn.

After starting the European day at a 32-month high on the mark, the greenback got a hefty push higher mid-afternoon when German chancellor Helmut Kohl said that Germany and Italy were both working towards monetary union.
Markets sold marks on the view that Italy's potential inclusion in the European single currency, set for launch in 1999, would undermine the stability of the new euro.

Kohl's comments were seen as the final word in a simmering row which broke out this week over a newspaper report claiming a secret deal had been struck to keep Italy out of European monetary union for the first year or so.
With foreign exchange markets labelled by Rubin as a "principal topic" for the G7 agenda, other less controversial issues seem likely to gain scant attention.
Other agenda items include debt relief to the world's poorest countries and cooperation between supervisory authorities.

On the dollar, the dilemma will be how to welcome the currency's recovery from 1995 lows -- which the G7 itself has fostered -- without sending a signal to the market which could prompt a further surge or a slide lower.

"Their aim will be to try to smooth the market movements," Eckhard Schulte, economist at the Industrial Bank of Japan in Frankfurt, said of the Group of Seven which comprises Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.
"They want to see a more gradual movement," he added.

Friday's surge was triggered by German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who said the strong dollar helped boost German exports, posed no inflation risk and that there was no need for the G7 to set exchange rate targets.

The United States and France in particular have joined Germany in welcoming the dollar's rise. But Japan, which has seen the yen fall by over 50 percent against the dollar in the last 22 months, has repeatedly expressed concern about the rapid move in currency rates and called for G7 action against it.
Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka repeated on Friday that he would be stressing the need for exchange rate stability at the meeting.

Even International Monetary Fund head Michel Camdessus, who this week said currency levels were extremely favourable, warned on Friday that the yen should not be allowed to fall so far as to force Japan to raise interest rates.
